Y562 is the export code for a loose ripe pu’er from Yunnan, which drinkers nicknamed the “little black box” after its carton. The Jixing mark on the front shows a tiger coming downhill. The box was made to carry the province’s own brand. Much of Yunnan’s loose pu’er once travelled in bulk, and in Japan importers repacked it under their own labels. In 1980 Yunnan brought packaging and tea export designers together to change that, so Y562 carried Chinese lettering on the front and “Superior Yunnan Pu-erh Tea” on the back.

Tang Zheng drew the tiger from an openwork jade pendant, and Yin Huize framed the lettering with patterns taken from Chinese lacquerware. The two took cartons painted by hand to the spring Canton Fair, and buyers ordered from those samples. Pu’er magazine describes the original blend as grades five and six of ripe tea from Menghai Tea Factory. Its yellow box companion, Y671, used grades six and seven from Kunming Tea Factory.

This box dates from 1993, twenty years after Yunnan’s state factories brought the wet pile into production, which places it in the style’s third decade. At thirty-three years it counts as aged ripe pu’er. The leaf keeps changing with the air and moisture around it, so its storage has shaped it as much as its age.
28436463-2272-4f68-83e1-b6d86f798be2: This ripe pu’er brick is from Yunnan and dates to 1990. Ripe pu’er gets its character from wet piling, a process in which damp tea leaves ferment before the tea is dried.
